title: Rooks on the seventh rank
summary: Penetrate to the seventh rank, attack pawns from the side, and confine the king.

steps.md:
A rook on the **seventh rank** (second rank for Black) attacks pawns that are still on their starting squares, from the side where they are weakest, and **cuts the king off on the back rank**. Two rooks there ("pigs") often force mate or perpetual check; with the enemy king on the eighth rank this is the "absolute seventh".

How to get there: control an **open file**, then use an entry square on it (often supported by a pawn or covered so the opponent cannot contest it).

steps.question: Why is the seventh rank so strong in endgames?
choices: Pawns there have not moved, so they can only be defended by pieces, and the enemy king is confined to the back rank
Because rooks move faster on the seventh
Because it is close to promotion
steps.explain: Pawns on their starting squares cannot defend each other along a rank; the rook attacks them one by one. Meanwhile the enemy king cannot come forward to help. Capablanca valued a rook on the seventh worth about a pawn.

steps.prompt: White to move. Your rook is on the seventh and your d-pawn is one step from queening. Find the quiet move that decides.
steps.explain: **34.Rc7!** prepares Rc8+: the rook leaves b7 to a square from which it can check on the back rank. After 34...Kh7 35.Rc8 the rook covers c8/d8 and the pawn queens. The seventh rank and the passed pawn work together.

steps.question: Both sides have a rook and an open file. Your opponent offers to trade rooks on the file. When should you avoid the trade and fight for the seventh instead?
choices: When you can occupy the file first and your rook will reach the seventh with tempo or create threats there
Only when you are material down
steps.explain: Control of the only open file decides who reaches the seventh. If you can double rooks or occupy the entry square first, keep the rooks; if the opponent controls it, trading may be wise.

steps.question: Two rooks on your seventh rank, enemy king on g8, enemy pawns on f7, g7 and h7, no other defenders. What should you look for first?
choices: Checks and captures: Rxf7, Rxg7+ and back-rank ideas often lead to mate or perpetual check
steps.explain: Doubled rooks on the seventh ("pigs") eat pawns with gain of tempo and create mating nets against a king trapped on the eighth rank. Calculate the forcing captures first.

steps.question: Your rook controls the open d-file, but Black covers d7 and d8 with king and rook. How do you usually get to the seventh rank?
choices: Double rooks on the file, or switch to another open file where the entry square is not covered
Play Rd7 anyway and lose the rook
steps.explain: An open file is only useful if it has an **entry square**. Doubling adds an attacker on the entry square; a second open file stretches the defender (Nimzowitsch: the file is the road, the seventh rank is the goal).

steps.md: **Retrieval check.** What two things does a rook on the seventh do? (Attack unmoved pawns, confine the king.) What do you need before you can get there? (Control of an open file and an entry square.)

sources: Nimzowitsch, My System (1925), the seventh and eighth ranks
